passage:
Class teacher's note, 9B, Wednesday. Jomon.
At the end of the day, while I was packing test papers, Divyansh hovered at my desk. "Sir, can I talk to you? It's kind of serious." My first instinct was to say, "Tomorrow, I'm late." I'm glad I didn't. He told me he hasn't slept properly for weeks, that his chest tightens every morning at the school gate, and that he's scared his parents will think he's making excuses for his marks. I put the papers down and said, "Thank you for telling me. That took courage." I gave him no speech about studying harder.
What I did next: I walked him to the school counsellor's room before she left, and with his permission I phoned his mother, who came in that evening. As he left, Divyansh asked if he could come back to me if it got worse. I said yes. I think he will.

qa.q: What was Jomon doing when Divyansh came to the desk?
qa.a: Packing test papers.

qa.q: What was Divyansh scared of?
qa.a: That his parents would think he was making excuses for his marks.

qa.q: Which moment decided how this conversation went?
qa.a: Jomon chose not to say "Tomorrow, I'm late", put the papers down and thanked Divyansh, then walked him to the counsellor.

qa.q: What might have happened if Jomon had said "Tomorrow"?
qa.a: Divyansh might have felt dismissed and never asked again, carrying the fear alone.

grounding: It shows a teacher whom a teenager finally approaches staying calm, thanking him and acting without a lecture, so the boy is willing to ask again.

passage:
Thursday night.
Pankaj stayed back after tabla class today, tuning and retuning the same drum. Then he said, very fast, "Tanvir Sir, I've been feeling really low for months and I don't know who to tell." My first thought was the old lecture I got at his age: focus, practise more, stop brooding. I swallowed it. I said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you chose me."
He talked for a long while. He's skipping school some days, can't enjoy even music, and he's scared his father will call it drama. I didn't argue or promise it would pass by itself. I asked if we could call his mother together. We did, from my verandah, and she came to fetch him. She's booking the family doctor for tomorrow and asked me to come along if Pankaj wants.
Before he left he said, "Can I talk to you again if it gets bad?"
"Any time," I said.

qa.q: From where did they call Pankaj's mother?
qa.a: From Tanvir's verandah.

qa.q: What was Pankaj afraid of, and what shows he was nervous?
qa.a: Pankaj was scared his father would call it drama; he kept tuning and retuning the same drum and then spoke very fast.

qa.q: Which choice in Tanvir's first moment shaped the whole conversation?
qa.a: Tanvir swallowed the old lecture and thanked Pankaj instead, then listened and called Pankaj's mother together with him.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's last question show about how the first response felt to him?
qa.a: It shows he felt safe and taken seriously, so he is willing to ask again.

grounding: It shows a music teacher receiving a teenager's request for help calmly, thanking him and acting the same day, so the student feels able to return.

subtype: Adult receiving a request for help [Receiver]
passage: I'm Deepak, and I've taught maths for twelve years. What I remember most is a Tuesday in October. Nitin, a quiet boy in Class 10, stayed after class and said, "Sir, I don't think I'm okay. I can't stop feeling scared." I wanted to say, "It's just board exam stress, everyone feels it." I stopped myself. I put down my chalk, sat on the bench beside him and said, "Thank you for telling me. That took courage." I listened without lecturing. Then I said, "Let's go to the counsellor now, together." She saw him that period, and with his agreement, called his parents. Months later, Nitin told me he'd almost not come to me. If I'd brushed him off, he'd never have asked anyone again.

qa.q: What month did Nitin approach Deepak?
qa.a: October.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when he wanted to say it was just exam stress?
qa.a: He felt tempted to brush it off but checked himself, choosing calm care instead.

qa.q: What did Deepak do that made his response effective?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked Nitin, listened without lecturing and took him straight to the counsellor, who involved his parents.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt if Deepak had dismissed him?
qa.a: Nitin might have felt ashamed and alone and never asked anyone for help again.

grounding: Shows a teacher approached by a struggling teenager who stays calm, thanks him and acts without lecturing, knowing the first response shapes whether he asks again.

Sunday: Gautam, fifteen, stood in the doorway. "Papa, can I talk to you?" Lalit, watching cricket, said, "Later, beta, last over." Gautam went back to his room.
Wednesday: Lalit noticed Gautam hadn't eaten dinner. That night Gautam came again. "Papa, I'm not okay. I think I need help." Lalit felt a jolt. He switched off the television and turned fully towards him. "Thank you for telling me. Sit, I'm listening." He didn't lecture or say, "At your age we just got on with it." He listened. Then he said, "Tomorrow I'll call the school counsellor. We'll go together."
Friday: After the first session, Gautam said in the car, "I almost didn't ask you again, after Sunday." Lalit swallowed. "I'm glad you did."

qa.a: Cricket.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel when Gautam said he wasn't okay?
qa.a: He felt a jolt of worry and gave Gautam his full, calm attention.

qa.a: He stopped everything, thanked Gautam, listened without lecturing and arranged a counsellor the next day.

qa.q: How might Gautam have felt after being told "later" on Sunday?
qa.a: Gautam likely felt dismissed and discouraged, nearly deciding not to ask again.

passage: "Santosh, you asked what a new teacher should do when a child comes for help. Let me tell you two stories. My first year as a teacher, a girl named Rekha came to me crying. 'Ma'am, I can't cope.' I said, 'Everyone is stressed, study harder.' She never came to me again. I think about her still. Years later, a boy named Imtiaz knocked on my staff room door. I remembered Rekha. I put down my pen. I said, 'Thank you for telling me.' I let him speak without interrupting. Then I walked him to the counsellor myself, and we called his mother together. He finished school and still sends me a card each Diwali. That first answer, Santosh, decides everything." Kavitha folded her hands.

qa.q: What did Kavitha tell Rekha?
qa.a: 'Everyone is stressed, study harder.'

qa.q: How does Kavitha feel about what happened with Rekha?
qa.a: She feels regretful and still troubled, thinking about Rekha years later.

qa.q: What choice in the second story made the difference?
qa.a: Kavitha stayed calm, thanked Imtiaz, listened without interrupting and walked him to the counsellor, calling his mother.

qa.q: How might Rekha have felt after Kavitha's reply?
qa.a: Rekha likely felt dismissed and alone, which is why she never came back.

passage:
The final bell had gone, the rain was pelting down and Raghav Sir had exactly ten minutes before the staff bus left. He was stuffing papers into his bag when Pranav appeared at the staffroom door, soaked.
"Sir, can I… talk? It's nothing, maybe."
Raghav Sir glanced at the clock. Then he put the bag down. "Come in. I've got time."
Pranav sat and stared at the table. "I've been feeling really low. For weeks. I can't sleep. I didn't know who to tell."
Raghav Sir didn't lecture or say "it's just exam stress." He said, "Thank you for telling me. That took courage." He texted the counsellor, who was still in the building, and walked Pranav to her room himself. Then he called Pranav's mother, with Pranav's agreement, before leaving.
He missed the bus. He took an auto home and didn't mind.

qa.q: How much time did Raghav Sir have before the staff bus left?
qa.a: Exactly ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Raghav Sir feeling when Pranav appeared at the door?
qa.a: He felt a moment of pressure about the bus, then calm concern and gratitude that Pranav chose to trust him.

qa.q: What did Raghav Sir do well as the adult Pranav approached?
qa.a: He stayed calm, thanked Pranav, didn't lecture or dismiss, and acted at once by taking him to the counsellor and calling his mother.

qa.q: What would change if Raghav Sir had said "Not now, I have a bus"?
qa.a: Pranav might feel dismissed and never ask for help again, carrying the low feeling alone.
